what_its_for: Amitriptyline is used to treat depression. It may also be prescribed for nerve pain, migraines, sleep problems, or anxiety, even though these are not always listed on the label. It belongs to a group of medicines called tricyclic antidepressants, which help balance certain chemicals in your brain.
how_to_take: Take amitriptyline exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or a glass of milk. Because it can make you feel drowsy, your doctor may have you take your full dose at bedtime. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablet unless your doctor says it is okay.
dosing: Doses vary a lot depending on why you are taking this medicine. A common starting dose for adults is 25 mg to 75 mg per day, which may be taken all at once at bedtime or split into smaller doses throughout the day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time, up to 150 mg per day or more in some cases. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store amitriptyline at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medication in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you no longer need this medicine, ask your pharmacist about the best way to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking amitriptyline. Alcohol can make drowsiness and dizziness much worse and can be dangerous. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid getting too hot or becoming dehydrated — amitriptyline can make it harder for your body to cool down. Tell your doctor or dentist about all your medications before any surgery or dental work. Do not stop taking amitriptyline suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: thoughts of harming yourself or suicide, unusual changes in mood or behavior, chest pain or a fast or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting, difficulty urinating, seizures, high fever with stiff muscles, confusion, or sweating (signs of a rare but serious reaction called serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome), yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if you notice increased depression, agitation, or anxiety, especially in the first few weeks of treatment or after a dose change. Note: The FDA requires a warning that antidepressants may increase suicidal thoughts in children, teenagers, and young adults, especially when first starting treatment.
when_it_works: Amitriptyline does not work overnight. For depression, it may take 2 to 4 weeks before you start to feel better, and sometimes up to 6 to 8 weeks for the full benefit. For pain or migraine prevention, it may also take several weeks to notice improvement. It is important to keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults: Amitriptyline is generally NOT recommended for people over 65 because it can cause serious side effects like confusion, falls, memory problems, and heart issues. Ask your doctor about safer alternatives. Children and teenagers: This medicine is not usually given to children under 12. Young people taking antidepressants need to be watched closely for mood changes or suicidal thoughts. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine should only be used during pregnancy if your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk. Breastfeeding: Amitriptyline passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
